newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - March 7.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - March 7.

text.p: The following stories were reported in Friday's electronic version of The Wall Street Journal:

* Great Western Financial agreed to be acquired by Washington Mutual for stock in a deal valued at $6.6 billion, but H.F. Ahmanson, which had made a hostile bid for the Los Angeles-based thrift, is expected to raise its offer.
* Opinions vary over how much Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan should be saying about the stock market, as his recent comments have annoyed small investors and some traders.

* ITT agreed to sell its half of Madison Square Garden, the New York Knicks, the New York Rangers and MSG Cablevision network to its partner, Cablevision Systems, for $650 million in cash and options and $115 million in assumed debt.
* China made a further concession to join the World Trade Organization, saying it would give Chinese companies the right to trade directly with foreign companies.
* Walt Disney's ABC television network shifted ABC News President Roone Arledge into the new position of ABC News Chairman.
* Stocks in Germany, France, Britain and neighboring countries rose to new highs on the continued strength of the U.S. dollar, which hit a 35-month high against the mark.
* Major retailers posted stronger-than-expected sales in February, with sales rising for all segments except consumer electronics and home-improvement items.
* Wal-Mart said it will buy back $2 billion of its stock and increase its dividend by 29 percent.
* Chrysler hired Equis Corp, a Chicago-based real estate firm, to improve the performance of its global real estate holdings, valued at $8 billion.

* The U.S. Tax Court upheld a decision by the Internal Revenue Service refusing to let Colgate-Palmolive claim nearly $100 million in losses from a tax-shelter partnership the company formed with the help of Merrill Lynch.

* An advertising group is lobbying against a government proposal to auction off vanity toll-free numbers on the new "888" exchange to businesses, saying similar numbers could cause confusion and chaos.
* Initial claims for jobless benefits last week fell sharply, and orders to U.S. factories rose 2.5 percent in January.
* A Texas jury said Honda Motor is one-third responsible in a $30 million verdict issued in the case of a young driver who died after his Honda all-terrain vehicle flipped.
* Arthur Andersen started an information-technology division to focus on audits and services for electronic commerce transactions.
* Schuller Corp, a Denver maker of insulation and building materials, has also been insulating its profits from taxes.

Schuller gets an array of unusual tax deductions, artifacts of asbestos litigation and the 1982 bankruptcy-law filing of its predecessor, Manville Corp. These deductions make Schuller "a perpetual cash-generating machine" for the next decade, says Gary Schneider, a bullish Bear, Stearns & Co analyst -- and one of the few analysts following the stock.
Why, then, the recent discontent among some longstanding investors? -- Heard on the Street.
* Bond traders warily approached the one-year anniversary of one of the biggest monthly U.S. payroll gains on record by driving prices lower. --Credit Markets.
--New York newsdesk 212-859-1610
